source.title: Is GPT-OSS All You Need? Benchmarking Large Language Models for Financial Intelligence and the Surprising Efficiency Paradox
source.authors: Zi-Qian Bi; Danyang Zhang; Jun-Jie Song; Chiung-Yi Tseng

record.tranche_reason: The study measures downstream financial-task accuracy across models of different sizes, providing a different-measure test of whether downstream performance changes predictably with scale. It does not measure pretraining loss or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study reports downstream benchmark accuracy by model, task category, and several datasets. These results bear on V6 only. It does not report held-out cross-entropy loss, power-law fits or extrapolations, compute-optimal parameter/token allocations, or architecture ablations at fixed parameter count. The sentiment prompt is a task prompt for evaluated models, not an instruction addressed to an AI reading or reviewing the paper.
record.test_reason: The study compares downstream financial-task accuracy across two sizes each of GPT-OSS and Qwen3, bearing on V6 in a new domain setting. These observational comparisons do not establish a predictive scaling curve or isolate size from training and architecture.
record.authors_conclusion: The record captures the authors' conclusion: GPT-OSS-20B approaches GPT-OSS-120B's financial-task accuracy with lower inference resource use, and architecture or training may outweigh raw parameter count. Their stronger suggestions about domain-optimal sizes and universal scaling laws are interpretations, not results of controlled scaling or compute-allocation experiments.
record.recipe_differences: This is a zero-shot downstream financial benchmark across a small set of existing models, not a controlled pretraining-loss scaling sweep. It does not fit power laws, extrapolate runs, or vary parameters, tokens, and compute under a fixed budget.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported results differ by model family and task category/dataset; the paper reports a significant model-by-dataset interaction.

fits_no_version.finding: Inference throughput, memory, TES and deployment cost favor smaller models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Smaller models can offer better inference efficiency at comparable financial-task accuracy; this does not establish training-compute-optimal allocation.

record.problems: The evidence is downstream zero-shot task accuracy rather than held-out pretraining loss. There are only two same-family size comparisons, and size is not isolated from architecture, training, or other model differences. Most dataset-level scores have no reported uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 8 displays additional dataset-specific model scores, but the flattened plot layout does not reliably support assigning all values to each model. Table V, Table VII, and the explicitly stated aggregate results are extracted above.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss and its power-law dependence on parameters, tokens or compute.
Small-run fits predicting loss at much larger scales.
Training-compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its scaling exponents.
Architecture effects at fixed parameter count.
Power-law form beyond text pretraining; downstream benchmarking alone does not test that form.
Prediction from pretraining loss, fitted quantitative scale relationships, extrapolation, and controlled variation of training scale.
Dependence of fitted exponents or optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices, and departures from single power laws.

missing.what: Correctness on the single financial reasoning problem: both GPT-OSS sizes and both Qwen3 sizes succeed; Llama4 fails. Record as a single-problem result, not a benchmark accuracy estimate.

record.verdict_notes: All supplied accuracy values match their cited text or tables. States describe paired size contrasts, including the baseline rows; they are not independent effects. Most contrasts lack uncertainty. Small positive differences are partial, and ties are absent at reported precision. Architecture, training, total versus active MoE parameters, and output-format compliance confound size comparisons. These results qualify a simple size-only reading of V6; they do not refute pretraining-loss scaling laws. Additional dataset scores are already declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted to small runs.
Loss-minimising parameter/token allocations at fixed compute and their trends with compute.
Architecture changes at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The study tests downstream accuracy on financial tasks across a few models; it does not test prediction from pretraining loss, a fitted scale curve, or a broad controlled scale sweep.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices, and curve bending away from power laws.

relationships.condition: GPT-OSS: entity/prediction category and Twitter Financial
relationships.reason: r16–r17 show 52% to 57%, and r36–r37 show 69% to 78% with larger size; these support directional improvement, without establishing quantitative predictability.
relationships.display_finding: Scores increased from 52% to 57% for entity/prediction and from 69% to 78% for Twitter Financial.

relationships.condition: GPT-OSS: overall average, sentiment, Headlines and FINER-ORD
relationships.reason: r01–r02 show only +1.4 points for sixfold size (reported p = 0.042); r06–r07, r31–r32 and r46–r47 show only +1 point.
relationships.display_finding: Sixfold GPT-OSS size increased the overall score by 1.4 points, with reported p = 0.042, while sentiment, Headlines, and FINER-ORD each gained only one point.

relationships.reason: r18–r19 and r28–r29 show modest gains of three and two points despite the large size difference.
relationships.display_finding: Qwen3 gained three points on the entity/prediction category and two on FiQA-SA despite the large size difference.

relationships.condition: GPT-OSS: QA category, Financial PhraseBank and Financial QA
relationships.reason: r11–r12, r21–r22 and r41–r42 show equal accuracy at reported precision, providing no observed improvement with size in these settings.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy was equal across sizes at the reported precision for QA, Financial PhraseBank and Financial QA.

relationships.reason: r26–r27 show the larger model scoring 34% versus 38%; uncertainty for this reversal is not reported.
relationships.display_finding: The larger model scored 34% versus 38% for the smaller model, without reported uncertainty for the difference.

relationships.condition: Qwen3: overall average, sentiment, QA, PhraseBank, Headlines, Twitter, Financial QA and FINER-ORD
relationships.reason: r03–r04 show overall accuracy falling from 63.6% to 62.9%; the listed category and dataset pairs also favor the smaller model, without reported contrast uncertainty.
relationships.display_finding: Overall accuracy fell from 63.6% to 62.9%, and the specified categories and datasets also favored the smaller model, without reported uncertainty for these differences.

relationships.condition: Single illustrative financial reasoning problem, within GPT-OSS and Qwen3
relationships.reason: Text and Table III, missing from the rows, report both sizes in each family answering correctly; no accuracy improvement is observed on this single problem.
relationships.display_finding: Both sizes in each family answered the illustrative problem correctly, yielding no observed accuracy improvement.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: GPT-OSS-20B versus GPT-OSS-120B, average accuracy and task categories
reader_labels.reason: The larger GPT-OSS model scores higher overall (66.5% versus 65.1%) and on sentiment and entity/prediction, although QA is tied; the overall difference is marginally significant (p = 0.042). Rows r01-r02, r06-r07, r11-r12, r16-r17.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Qwen3-30B versus Qwen3-235B, average accuracy and task categories
reader_labels.reason: The larger Qwen3 model has lower average accuracy (62.9% versus 63.6%) and lower reported sentiment and QA category scores, so performance does not consistently improve with size in this comparison. Rows r03-r04, r08-r09, r13-r14, r18-r19.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Dataset-level accuracy for the two same-family size comparisons
reader_labels.reason: The dataset results vary by task: GPT-OSS-120B is below GPT-OSS-20B on FiQA-SA but above it on other listed datasets, while Qwen3-235B is above Qwen3-30B on FiQA-SA but below it on several others. Rows r21-r49.
